My question however is this: what is the difference between programming languages?

I have zero knowledge of any language, so where should I start, and how should I start? Codecademy isn't the est imo. Want to learn programming, and python was suggested to me

Generally speaking, the easier a language is to learn / use, the less efficient it is. There is generally a tradeoff in performance.

In most cases, you can spare a magnitude of cpu cycles, because processors are really fast these days. So, Python is a good language to learn because when you are learning, you aren't going to be working on projects that require a great deal of efficiency.

Likewise, there are a number of professions which don't require efficient code. Web development is one of these. So, Python is not only easy to learn, but there is also high demand for it in the market place.

Python is certainly a good language to start with, it's easy to find good tooling for it and it's quite well designed in that if something is wrong it will throw an exception (i.e. complain to you) instead of silently returning a wrong or unexpected value.

With regard to more powerful and less powerful, well, it's not really true that any programming language (technically, any turing complete language) can express any programs that another programming language cannot. However there's a big difference in how easy it is to do certain things, so programming languages can be more or less powerful for a given task.

Programming languages also have different performance characteristics. Python is known to produce programs that run relatively slowly. It's fast enough for most tasks but you don't want to write very performance intensive code in.

There are lots of libraries (collections of already written code) for Python that you can use, which often makes it much easier to do something in Python than in another language, no need to invent the wheel again.

What you often see with Python is that libraries deal with performance intensive stuff by programming in C and making the result accessible from Python. So the programmer that uses those libraries can work in Python but still gets the performance benefits that come from C.

As for how to learn it. I can recommend exercism.io. That has a whole bunch of fairly simple Python exercises you can do and get feedback on. It's a great way to not just practice but also get advice on better ways to do stuff. (Disclaimer: I'm a contributor to exercism, though not the Python part)
